lines.text: A small, hot land at the mouth of the Red Sea, where ships and armies come and go. This is the story of Djibouti.
In 1888 the French founded a port on the coast, and named it Djibouti.
It became the capital of French Somaliland, and grew with the railway to Ethiopia.
Hassan Gouled Aptidon would become the first president of an independent Djibouti, and lead it for over twenty years.
Ismail Omar Guelleh would follow him in 1999, and lead the country ever since.
In 1967 the colony was renamed after its two main peoples, the French Territory of the Afars and the Issas.
Ten years later, in 1977, Djibouti became independent from France.
In 1991 the Afar rose in rebellion, and a civil war lasted three years.
In 2001, the United States set up Camp Lemonnier, one of several foreign military bases on this strategic shore.
And in 2016, a new railway to Addis Ababa, rebuilt by China, made Djibouti the gateway of Ethiopia.
Small in size, Djibouti stands guard where the Red Sea meets the ocean.
